newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria aims for budget of growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria aims for budget of growth in 1997.

text.p: After two years of trying to stabilise key facets of the Nigerian economy, military ruler General Sani Abacha is expected to unveil a fiscal budget for 1997 with a reflationary package to induce faster growth.

The World Bank and experts have praised the general for rescuing the economy, which plunged into crisis with other aspects of Nigerian life in 1993 when a presidential poll to restore democracy was annulled by his military predecessor.
"All the economic indices have worked beautifully for Nigeria," says Emmanuel Ijewere, president of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria.

But while achieving stability in the exchange rate and a rein on inflation to less than 30 percent from nearly 80 percent last December, growth in gross domestic product has been inadequate at three percent for Nigeria's 100 million people.
This is acknowledged by the government, which says it had to stabilise the economy before dashing for growth.

"At the end of 1994, Nigerians were well aware of the state of the economy and it was necessary to stabilise the economy before attempting for growth," Finance Minister Anthony Ani told a business forum in Lagos recently.
"The budget of 1995 was budget of renewal which encompassed re-building the economy while the budget of 1996 was a budget of consolidation," he said.
"In 1997, therefore, we shall be talking of a budget of growth and development, a budget of reflation without inflation, a budget of selective but productive reflation," he said.
The World Bank and central bank officials say they expect growth of up to 7.5 percent next year if the economic reforms in place now are maintained and improved upon.
But experts caution that the government must tread a fine line between stimulating growth and keeping inflation in check.
"Care still needs to be exercised as a surge in spending power will put pressure on both inflation and exchange rate," said David McKlean, head of Marina International Bank in Lagos.
Nigeria's annual budget is usually broadcast on New Year's Day, although Abacha has consistently delayed in releasing his budgets since he seized power in 1993.

After fixing exchange rates with disastrous consequences in 1994, Abacha the following year introduced the autonomous foreign exchange market as the main plank of an economic policy tagged "guided deregulation".

While economists have hailed the deregulation of exchange rates as good for business they have pointed to political instability as a key factor retarding economic progress in Nigeria, Sub-Saharan Africa's largest economy.
But analysts doubt that Abacha's budget broadcast would announce the release of political detainees, among whom are Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll.
Relations with many of Nigeria's traditional trading partners have soured over the slow pace of democratisation and concern at human rights abuses.

Having reaped bountifully from a boom in crude oil prices in 1996, Abacha should announce a hefty rise in oil income and say he will plough this into education, hospitals, roads and other public infrastructure for the benefit of ordinary people.
"I believe government should exempt anybody who earns below 35,000 naira ($437.5) per annum from any tax," said Ijewere.
The manufacturing industry, which is producing at less than 30 percent capacity, also expects a boost through incentives, such as lower taxes to reduce prices and spur consumer spending.
According to the finance minister, another major policy initiative to stimulate growth and induce physical development would be privatisation of some big state enterprises.

"Privatisation of government-owned enterprises will free resources tied up in such ventures for social development. Government in embarking on its privatisation programme in 1997 will ensure honesty, transparency and accountability," he says.
